questions.q: What separates a strategist from a fool, according to the summary?
a: The strategist knows how the battle will be won before it starts
The strategist fights more battles than anyone else
The strategist relies on superior numbers
The strategist waits for the enemy to attack first
questions.why: Lesson 1 says fools fight and then look for a way to win, while strategists plan the win in advance.

questions.q: Why does the summary mention Bobby Fischer?
a: He withdrew after winning the world title and did not play for 20 years
He lost to a weaker opponent and retired in shame
He trained a group of young chess players
He wrote a book about military strategy
questions.why: Lesson 1 uses Fischer as an example of a great competitor who avoided further battles.

questions.q: What business lesson follows from the advice to avoid unwinnable battles?
a: Pick a niche where you can beat the competition instead of fighting the giant
Undercut every rival until they go out of business
Copy the market leader's product exactly
Avoid competition by staying very small
questions.why: Lesson 1 suggests that competing head-on with Coca-Cola is futile, but a targeted alternative could succeed.

questions.q: What does deception aim to achieve?
a: Making your opponent do what you want them to do
Making your opponent respect your strength
Hiding your product from customers
Delaying a battle until you are ready
questions.why: Lesson 2 says disguising strength and weakness is meant to impose your will on the enemy.

questions.q: How does the summary suggest leading a growing team?
a: Break it into small groups and steer them with clear signals
Give every person a detailed daily schedule
Keep all decisions with the founder alone
Add layers of managers as headcount grows
questions.why: Lesson 3 recommends small teams and clear signals, plus regular one-on-one contact.
